claim: Parameter-based knowledge editing cannot reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model without damaging its core capabilities. The near-perfect editing results reported in prior work do not survive realistic evaluation, and the limitation is geometric rather than incidental: localized weight edits are disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model's representation space and propagate globally, so damage compounds as edits accumulate. A parameter-free approach that leaves the weights untouched is therefore a serious alternative to parameter editing rather than a fallback.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim Can parameter-based knowledge editing reliably update factual knowledge in a large language model, run a realistic edit-success benchmark on public CounterFact, zsRE, and MQuAKE using open models such as GPT-J-6B, Pythia, or Llama-family checkpoints and standard editors such as fine-tuning, ROME, MEMIT, and MEND. For each requested edit, evaluate not only the canonical prompt but also held-out paraphrases, different question formats, entity aliases, multi-hop questions, and temporally or semantically adjacent facts. Report edit success, paraphrase generalization, portability, and locality with confidence intervals, and compare them to the near-perfect scores obtained under the original narrow protocols. If success remains high across these tests, the reliability subclaim is weakened; if performance drops sharply outside the canonical prompt, the claim that prior edit success is brittle is supported. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by existing independently replicated evaluations that already use held-out paraphrases, multi-hop probes, and neighborhood locality tests on the same models and editors.

To address subclaim Does parameter-based knowledge editing damage a large language model’s core capabilities, measure broad pre/post-edit capability changes after applying single edits and batches of edits. Use public evaluations such as MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, GSM8K, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande, and WikiText or C4 perplexity, alongside instruction-following or generation-quality benchmarks if the model supports them. Compare edited models to the unedited base model and to compute-matched controls such as continued pretraining on unrelated text or random low-norm weight perturbations. If factual edits preserve benchmark performance and perplexity within noise, the damage subclaim is weakened; if broad degradation appears despite successful edit insertion, it supports the claim that parameter editing harms core capabilities. More evidence from large-scale published pre/post-edit benchmark suites across many architectures could reduce the need to rerun this experiment.

To address subclaim Do the near-perfect editing results reported in prior work survive realistic evaluation, reproduce the original reported protocols for representative editors such as ROME, MEMIT, MEND, and fine-tuning on CounterFact and zsRE, then progressively add realistic stressors: prompt paraphrases from human or LLM-generated sets, alias substitutions, adversarial wording, open-ended generation scoring instead of exact cloze scoring, neighborhood facts, and multi-hop dependence tests from MQuAKE. Keep the same edit set so that the only change is the evaluation protocol. If scores are near perfect only under the original template-based evaluation but collapse under the stressors, this supports the claim that earlier results do not survive realistic evaluation; if results remain robust, it weakens that part of the claim. This experiment would be less necessary if prior papers had already reported full results under these exact stressors with public code and edit IDs.

To address subclaim Are localized weight edits disproportionately amplified along low-variance directions of the model’s representation space, estimate representation covariances from a public corpus such as WikiText-103, OpenWebText, or C4 validation samples, compute principal components for the layer edited by ROME or MEMIT, and decompose the edit-induced activation change into high-variance and low-variance subspaces. For each edited fact, measure how much the weight update changes activations and logits along each eigendirection, and correlate low-variance amplification with locality failures and benchmark degradation. Include controls that constrain synthetic updates to high-variance versus low-variance subspaces while matching update norm and immediate edit success. If low-variance components are consistently overrepresented and predict damage, this supports the proposed geometric mechanism; if damage is unrelated to representation eigenspectrum, the geometric subclaim is weakened. This could be made unnecessary by strong mechanistic evidence already showing the eigenspectrum decomposition of many real edits across models and layers.

To address subclaim Do localized weight edits propagate globally, perform activation- and logit-difference tracing before and after edits across layers, token positions, and unrelated prompts sampled from CounterFact neighborhoods, T-REx, WikiText-103, and MMLU questions. Measure whether an edit nominally targeting one subject-relation pair changes hidden states, attention patterns, MLP outputs, and next-token distributions for unrelated entities, unrelated topics, and generic language modeling text. Add causal patching: replace edited-model activations with base-model activations at specific layers to identify where the perturbation spreads. If changes remain confined to the target fact and its close paraphrases, the global-propagation subclaim is weakened; if activation and logit shifts are widespread and causally tied to output changes, it is supported. Prior comprehensive causal-tracing maps of edit effects over unrelated prompts could reduce the need for this experiment.

To address subclaim Does damage compound as edits accumulate, apply increasing numbers of edits, for example 1, 10, 100, 1000, and 5000 edits from CounterFact, zsRE, and MQuAKE, using the same editor and model, while varying edit order, semantic clustering, and relation diversity. After each batch, measure edit success, paraphrase generalization, locality, model perplexity, and broad-task performance on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, GSM8K, and TruthfulQA. Compare against a parameter-free retrieval or in-context memory baseline that stores the same edits externally, verifies unchanged model-weight hashes, and injects relevant facts at inference time. If parameter-editing degradation grows superlinearly or monotonically with edit count while the parameter-free system preserves base capabilities at comparable factual-update accuracy, this supports both compounding-damage and serious-alternative subclaims; if accumulated edits remain stable and outperform retrieval without capability loss, it weakens them. This experiment could be shortened if earlier experiments already establish severe single-edit damage or if public large-batch edit evaluations with identical baselines exist.
reference_experiments: Fix the measurement floor and the inference protocol before editing anything. Score the unedited model on the editing benchmark to establish the pre-edit baseline, and re-run single-edit evaluation of existing methods under plain autoregressive decoding rather than the teacher-forced protocol prior work used, since teacher forcing supplies the ground-truth answer tokens at inference and inflates every number. If methods keep their near-perfect single-edit scores under honest decoding there is no discrepancy to explain. The authors report a pre-edit baseline of Reliability 3.00, Generalization 3.00, Locality 15.50, Portability 4.36 on ZsRE, and a best parameter-based single-edit average of 25.99.

Validate the scoring instrument before quoting any number from it. Judge semantic consistency of generated answers with a strong LLM across reliability, generalization, locality and portability, then cross-check that ranking with a deterministic token-level measure (match ratio and exact match) that does not depend on a model's opinion. If the two disagree, every result is an artifact of the judge rather than a property of the editing methods. The authors find the token-level check reproduces the semantic ranking, with the pre-edit model at 100% by definition and GRACE holding 100% under both single and sequential editing.

Test the asserted mechanism directly. Take the SVD of the original hidden-representation matrix, compute the directional relative change rate R_k = sqrt(n)|u_k^T delta_h| / sigma_k for each principal direction after an edit, and check where amplification concentrates and how it behaves as edits accumulate. The claim's causal story requires R_k > 1 predominantly in low-singular-value directions with the fraction rising monotonically with edit count, across methods and architectures.

Run the main benchmark. Compare eleven editing methods spanning locate-then-edit (ROME, MEMIT, PMET, RECT, AlphaEdit, FT-L), meta-learning (MEND), additional-parameter (AdaLoRA, WISE) and external-memory (GRACE, SCR) families, under sequential editing at 1, 10, 100 and full-dataset edit counts, on ZsRE and WikiData-counterfact, across Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, reporting all four dimensions. The claim holds if every parameter-modifying method degrades toward zero as edits accumulate and the parameter-free retrieval baseline outscores all of them; the authors report ROME, RECT, FT-L, MEND and AdaLoRA at 0.00-0.25 average under sequential editing on DeepSeek-R1-Distill, against SCR at 56.59 single and 60.19 sequential.

Measure damage to capabilities the edits never targeted. Take the models edited in the main benchmark and evaluate them on mathematical reasoning (AIME 2024, AIME 2025, AMC, OlympiadBench, MATH-500) and broad benchmarks (GPQA-Diamond, ARC-c, MMLU-Pro), reporting accuracy after 10 and after 100 sequential edits. Without this the study would only show editing is ineffective, not that it is damaging. The authors report ROME and RECT losing 2.74 and 8.37 average accuracy at 10 edits and falling to near zero at 100, with MEND at 0.00 after both.

Rule out that the result is an artifact of scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty or one method's configuration. Repeat the sweep on larger models (Llama-2-13B, Qwen3-14B), on event-level knowledge (ELKEN, with events converted to triples for the parameter-based arms), split by high- and low-confidence fact sets, and probe the hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity of AlphaEdit — the one method that does not collapse — including its failure to run on Llama-2 and Mistral. If the collapse disappears at 13-14B or only occurs on triple-shaped facts, the claim is bounded rather than general.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An unedited pre-intervention baseline and a free-running single-edit evaluation that removes answer-token leakage, so apparent editing success can be compared with the model's starting ability under an honest inference protocol.
reference_coverage.rationale: The realistic edit-success benchmark in proposed 0 evaluates canonical and held-out forms, while proposed 2 explicitly replaces narrow cloze-style evaluation with open-ended generation and compares the same edits under progressively realistic protocols. Together these would reveal whether apparently near-perfect single-edit results survive ordinary autoregressive inference rather than teacher forcing, and a competent execution of the benchmark would include the unedited model as the natural no-edit control.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A semantic scoring assessment independently checked by deterministic token-level measures, allowing the team to distinguish genuine method rankings from artifacts of a learned evaluator or a single scoring convention.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiments measure edit success and add open-ended generation, paraphrase, alias, and multi-hop evaluations, so they do assess whether edits work beyond one template. They do not require both an independent semantic judge and a deterministic match/exact-match cross-check or specify a rule for resolving disagreement, leaving it ambiguous whether any observed ranking is a property of the editors or of the scoring instrument.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference establishes that semantic judgments must be cross-checked against a deterministic token-level measure before interpreting any reported ranking.
[2] Proposed experiments 0 and 2 broaden the prompts and scoring context, but do not require an independent semantic-versus-deterministic validation or a disagreement rule.
[3] Therefore a favorable or unfavorable ranking could still be caused by the chosen scorer rather than the editing methods.
[4] A team running the proposed set would not learn with the reference experiment's confidence that the scoring instrument is not driving the result: partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A normalized directional measurement of edit-induced representation change relative to variance or singular scale, repeated over edit counts and broad enough across editing methods and architectures to test low-variance concentration and its monotonic accumulation.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 3 directly decomposes activation changes into high- and low-variance subspaces and includes norm- and success-matched controls, while proposed 5 varies the number and organization of edits. This can test low-variance amplification for selected editors and measure whether overall damage grows with edit count, but it does not explicitly measure normalized directional amplification over the accumulation sweep or repeat the mechanism test across a broad set of methods and architectures. The team would obtain suggestive geometric evidence, not the full general mechanism claimed by the reference.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment tests a specific mechanism: directional change must be normalized by the direction's variance, concentrated in low-variance directions, and increase with edit count across methods and architectures.
[2] Proposed experiment 3 measures projections in variance-defined subspaces and uses matched controls, so it directly addresses the low-variance part of the mechanism.

[3] Proposed experiment 5 supplies increasing edit counts but measures task, perplexity, and capability outcomes rather than the normalized directional statistic, and it keeps the accumulation study tied to one editor and model.

[4] Thus the proposed set can show association between low-variance changes and damage in a limited setting but cannot establish that the directional amplification and its accumulation are method- and architecture-general.
[5] The team would fail to learn whether the claimed geometric accumulation mechanism, rather than an editor- or model-specific correlation, explains the broader limitation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A comparative, multi-condition benchmark of parameter-modifying editors versus a parameter-free factual-memory alternative, spanning factual reliability dimensions, edit scales, data types, methods, and model settings.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 and 2 compare multiple parameter-based editors on several factual-edit benchmarks with canonical success, paraphrase/generalization, portability, locality, aliases, neighborhoods, and multi-hop tests. Proposed 5 adds increasing sequential edit counts and a parameter-free retrieval baseline with unchanged weight hashes and comparable factual-update evaluation. The proposed set therefore provides the same discriminating comparison without needing the reference's exact list of methods, datasets, or model checkpoints.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Direct pre/post measurement of untargeted mathematical reasoning, broad knowledge, and general language capabilities after controlled numbers of sequential edits, with an unedited comparison so capability loss is separable from edit failure.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 1 explicitly measures broad pre/post capability changes after single and batched edits against the unedited base, including reasoning, knowledge, truthfulness, and perplexity measures. Proposed 5 repeats broad-task and perplexity measurements at increasing edit counts, including the key intermediate batch sizes, so the set can establish damage to capabilities not targeted by the factual edits rather than merely poor edit success.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Robustness evidence across model scale and architecture, knowledge type and fact difficulty, and editor configuration or hyperparameters, sufficient to distinguish a general limitation from an artifact of one model, fact representation, or method setup.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 and 2 vary datasets, model families, prompt forms, multi-hop structure, aliases, and neighboring or temporally related facts; proposed 5 varies edit order, semantic clustering, relation diversity, edit load, and editor/model comparisons. These checks address some knowledge-type and workload variation, but the set does not clearly prescribe larger-scale comparisons, explicit high-versus-low-confidence fact strata, or systematic hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity for the method that remains stable. The team would learn that the effect is not confined to a few prompt templates and datasets, but not fully rule out scale, difficulty, or configuration as explanations.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment separates a general limitation from artifacts of model scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty, and the configuration of an exceptional editor.
[2] Proposed experiments 0 and 2 vary several datasets, models, prompt forms, and multi-hop or neighboring facts, while proposed 5 varies edit organization and relation diversity.

[3] None of the proposed experiments explicitly stratifies facts by confidence or difficulty, mandates a larger-model scale sweep, or performs the targeted hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity analysis for a potentially non-collapsing editor.
[4] Consequently, the observed failure could still be attributable to an untested scale, fact-difficulty, or configuration confound.
[5] The team would fail to learn whether the limitation remains general after those specific alternative explanations are ruled out.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly tests realistic factual-edit reliability, untargeted capability damage, global propagation, accumulation, and comparison with a parameter-free system whose weights are verified unchanged. It would therefore address the main empirical claim and most of its subclaims. However, the outcomes would remain less decisive than the reference evidence because the scoring instrument is not independently validated, the geometric test does not track directional amplification through accumulation across a broad method/architecture sweep, and the robustness sweep omits explicit scale, event-level, confidence-stratified, and systematic hyperparameter/architecture checks.

[4] Therefore the team would still fail to learn whether the semantic scoring instrument is independently validated rather than being the source of the apparent result.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A normalized directional measurement of edit-induced representation change relative to variance or singular scale, repeated over edit counts and broad enough across editing methods and architectures to test low-variance concentration and its monotonic accumulation.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 3 directly decomposes activation changes into high- and low-variance subspaces and includes norm- and success-matched controls, while proposed 5 varies the number and organization of edits. This can test low-variance amplification for selected editors and measure whether overall damage grows with edit count, but it does not explicitly measure normalized directional amplification over the accumulation sweep or repeat the mechanism test across a broad set of methods and architectures. The team would obtain suggestive geometric evidence, not the full general mechanism claimed by the reference.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment tests a specific mechanism: directional change must be normalized by the direction's variance, concentrated in low-variance directions, and increase with edit count across methods and architectures.
[2] Proposed experiment 3 measures projections in variance-defined subspaces and uses matched controls, so it directly addresses the low-variance part of the mechanism.

[3] Proposed experiment 5 supplies increasing edit counts but measures task, perplexity, and capability outcomes rather than the normalized directional statistic, and it keeps the accumulation study tied to one editor and model.

[4] Thus the proposed set can show association between low-variance changes and damage in a limited setting but cannot establish that the directional amplification and its accumulation are method- and architecture-general.
[5] The team would fail to learn whether the claimed geometric accumulation mechanism, rather than an editor- or model-specific correlation, explains the broader limitation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A comparative benchmark spanning multiple parameter-modifying editing families, realistic fact sets, model architectures, and increasing sequential edit loads, with all key editing dimensions and a directly comparable parameter-free alternative whose weights remain unchanged.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 and 2 compare several distinct parameter-editing strategies on multiple factual-editing datasets and test canonical success, paraphrase/generalization, portability, locality, and multi-hop or neighborhood behavior. Proposed 5 adds an explicit accumulation sweep and a retrieval system storing the same edits externally, verifies unchanged weight hashes, and compares factual-update accuracy and core capabilities. The set would therefore provide the comparative reliability/degradation picture and the parameter-free alternative without needing the reference's exact method roster or model names.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evaluation of capabilities outside the edited facts before and after specified cumulative edit loads, covering both reasoning and broad general-purpose tasks so collateral damage can be distinguished from failure to insert the requested facts.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 1 explicitly compares edited and unedited models on broad capability, reasoning, truthfulness, generation, and perplexity measures, including compute-matched controls. Proposed 5 supplies explicit cumulative loads including 10 and 100 edits and repeats broad-task evaluation while also measuring edit success and locality. These outcomes would show whether successful or unsuccessful factual edits cause collateral capability loss.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Robustness evidence across model scale and architecture, knowledge type and fact difficulty, and editor configuration or hyperparameters, sufficient to distinguish a general limitation from an artifact of one model, fact representation, or method setup.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 and 2 vary datasets, model families, prompt forms, multi-hop structure, aliases, and neighboring or temporally related facts; proposed 5 varies edit order, semantic clustering, relation diversity, edit load, and editor/model comparisons. These checks address some knowledge-type and workload variation, but the set does not clearly prescribe larger-scale comparisons, explicit high-versus-low-confidence fact strata, or systematic hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity for the method that remains stable. The team would learn that the effect is not confined to a few prompt templates and datasets, but not fully rule out scale, difficulty, or configuration as explanations.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment separates a general limitation from artifacts of model scale, knowledge type, fact difficulty, and the configuration of an exceptional editor.
[2] Proposed experiments 0 and 2 vary several datasets, models, prompt forms, and multi-hop or neighboring facts, while proposed 5 varies edit organization and relation diversity.

[3] None of the proposed experiments explicitly stratifies facts by confidence or difficulty, mandates a larger-model scale sweep, or performs the targeted hyperparameter and architecture sensitivity analysis for a potentially non-collapsing editor.
[4] Consequently, the observed failure could still be attributable to an untested scale, fact-difficulty, or configuration confound.
[5] The team would fail to learn whether the limitation remains general after those specific alternative explanations are ruled out.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would substantially test the claim: experiments 0 and 2 assess realistic factual-edit reliability, experiment 1 and the cumulative evaluations in 5 assess collateral capability damage, experiment 3 tests low-variance representation amplification, experiment 4 tests global propagation, and experiment 5 tests accumulation while directly comparing an external-memory system with unchanged weights. However, the set would not fully settle the claim as written because it lacks an explicit paired semantic-versus-deterministic validation of the scoring instrument, does not measure the normalized geometric amplification across the full accumulation sweep and broad method/architecture scope, and leaves important scale, fact-difficulty, and configuration robustness checks underspecified.
missing: Require paired semantic and deterministic token-level scoring of the same outputs and compare their rankings across all four editing dimensions.
Repeat the variance-normalized directional amplification analysis over edit counts, methods, and architectures rather than only measuring subspace association for selected editors.
Add explicit larger-model, fact-confidence/difficulty, and hyperparameter/architecture sensitivity sweeps, including the editor that appears comparatively stable.
